markingScheme.criterion: Quotes at least two of the student's own logged Meteor Chain Launcher trials (different rock sizes with their different outcomes) as evidence.
markingScheme.accept: Any two genuine size/outcome pairs from the student's own Investigation Record trials; exact wording not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: A general claim ('bigger rocks survive') with no actual logged trials quoted.

markingScheme.criterion: Explains the underlying mechanism: friction with the atmosphere at very high speed heats and burns/vaporizes the rock, and a bigger rock has more mass/material so there is more of it left after burning, giving it a better chance of surviving to the ground.
markingScheme.accept: Any scientifically valid phrasing of atmospheric friction/heat burning the rock, and size affecting how much material is left; exact keywords not required.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'small rocks burn up and big ones don't' with no mention of friction/heat or of size/mass as the reason why.

markingScheme.criterion: Correctly uses the vocabulary chain: names the object a meteoroid before atmospheric entry, a meteor while it is streaking/burning, and (only for the trial where a piece reached the ground) a meteorite.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct use of at least two of the three terms in the right place in the chain.
markingScheme.insufficient: Using only one term (e.g. calling everything 'a meteor') or using a term in the wrong stage.

markingScheme.criterion: Identifies the specific error: a 'shooting star' (a meteor) is the streak of light itself, produced by a rock burning up in the atmosphere — it is the burning that is seen, not a landing, so what is seen in the sky and what (if anything) reaches the ground are not automatically the same event.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that a meteor is the burning streak of light, not the object landing.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'that's not really a star' with no explanation of what a shooting star actually is.

markingScheme.criterion: States that only a genuine surviving fragment that reaches the ground is properly called a meteorite, and that this is rare — most meteoroids burn up completely and nothing lands at all.
markingScheme.accept: Any correct statement that most meteors leave nothing behind, and that a real meteorite landing is uncommon.
markingScheme.insufficient: Saying 'meteorites are different from meteors' with no mention of rarity or of most burning up completely.

markingScheme.criterion: Gives a plausible, reasoned correct account of what probably really happened (e.g. the friend saw a meteor overhead that burned up completely with nothing landing nearby, or something unrelated landed and was mistakenly connected to the meteor) rather than just asserting the friend is wrong.
markingScheme.accept: Any scientifically reasonable alternative account, clearly connected to what a meteor/meteorite actually is.
markingScheme.insufficient: Stating only 'they are wrong' with no attempt to say what probably happened instead.

markingInstructions: Mark ONLY the two constructed responses (Explain, Apply). Award marks point-by-point using each question's marking_scheme in marking_context: each point is worth the marks stated, is independent unless it names a dependsOn point (in which case only award it if that earlier point was also awarded), and each point's 'accept'/'insufficient' tell you exactly what does and doesn't count. use_of_evidence's 3 marks ARE the Explain marking_scheme's 3 points, and reasoning's 3 marks ARE the Apply marking_scheme's 3 points — the rubric levels restate the same points as bands; award each set of 3 marks ONCE, not twice. communication is a separate, holistic 2 marks across both answers' clarity and vocabulary, never overlapping with the content marks. Copy auto_marked_score into knowledge_accuracy (7 marks = full). Use the student's own logged Investigation Record (the station/item/outcome columns in simulation_results.trials, especially the Meteor Chain Launcher rows) to check that any claim they make about their own results is consistent with what they actually did. Accept scientifically valid alternative wording and do not penalise spelling unless meaning is unclear. Total is out of 15 (7 auto + 3 + 3 + 2); report the percentage, one strength, one correction, and one next step, in under 80 words.
